dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Good morning, Dr. Lee. Sorry if I seem a bit quiet today.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Good morning, Anthony. It’s nice to see you. How are you feeling as we start our session?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: It’s been one of those days where the morning coffee feels heavier than usual. I stayed late at the branch last night reviewing the portal for a rate lock I was supposed to secure.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Staying late can be draining. You mentioned a rate lock—what was the plan you had in mind for that?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: The credit‑union was offering a 9 % promotional APR on the new card. I set a reminder for 5 pm, because the cut‑off is strict. I watched the screen until after midnight, refreshing every minute, convinced the system would hold the rate until I hit ‘confirm.’

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like you invested a lot of energy into making sure the lock went through. When the clock turned over, what actually happened?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: When I finally logged back in at 2 am, the rate had already leapt to 19 %. I felt this sudden pressure in my chest, like the floor disappearing under me. It hit me hard because I’m the one who tells members, ‘we’ve got your back.’

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That contrast between what you promise and what you experienced must have been stark. What thoughts ran through your mind at that moment?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I started thinking I’m a fraud. If I can’t lock a stable rate for my own card, how can I guarantee anything to the people who rely on me?

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: You’re describing a deep sense of disappointment in yourself. Earlier, you said you set the reminder and watched the portal like a watchdog. What does that tell us about how you usually approach your work?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I’m always organized—checklists, logs, timestamps. I like to have a clear audit trail. It’s how I keep my own standards aligned with the policies I draft for members.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: So the system’s failure felt like a violation of the very standards you set for yourself and others. How did that affect your feeling of control over the situation?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Even though I was scrolling the server log every second, I still felt powerless. Seeing that 0.02‑second lag at 5:01 pm was like a tiny crack in a wall I thought was solid.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: A small crack can feel huge when the structure is something you rely on. It sounds like you’re wrestling with both the technical glitch and the emotional impact of it.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Exactly. My throat tightens when anyone mentions the jump. I replay the 19 % flashing on my screen over and over, and I can’t shake the feeling that everyone in the branch heard it.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That physical reaction—tight throat, replaying the image—suggests the event is triggering a deeper alarm for you. When you think about the promise you make to members, what are you hoping to prove for yourself?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I want to prove that I walk the same road I set for members. If I can lock the 9 % for my own card, I can tell them I’m not just talking theory.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: So there’s a desire to model the behavior you recommend. It’s understandable to want that consistency. What might be a realistic way to keep that consistency, even when the system hiccups?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Maybe I need a backup—something beyond the timer. I could set a phone alarm for 4:55 pm and also email myself a screenshot of the rate before I click confirm.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds like a concrete safety net. It respects your organized style while giving you a second layer of confirmation.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I like that. It feels less like I’m trusting a single point of failure and more like I’m covering all bases.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Having multiple checks can also reduce the intensity of that knot in your throat, because the responsibility is shared with the tools you set up.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I’m going to program the alarm, draft a quick email template, and maybe even jot a note in my planner to verify the timestamp manually. That way, if the system slips again, I’ve already covered the gap.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like you’re turning a painful experience into an opportunity to refine your process. How do you think this will affect the way you talk to members about rate locks moving forward?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I can be honest about the extra steps I take, which might actually build more trust. I won’t have to pretend the system is infallible; I’ll show that I’m prepared for its quirks.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That honesty can be a strength. It aligns the promise you give with the reality you manage. Is there anything else you’d like to explore about how this event impacted your sense of competence?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I guess I need to remember that a single slip doesn’t equal overall failure. I’m still the person who’s built the deadline system for others. I just need to give myself a bit of the same leeway.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That’s a compassionate perspective—extending the same standards you set for members to yourself. Shall we check in next week to see how the new reminders are working for you?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Sounds good. I’ll have the alarm and email set up by tomorrow, and I’ll let you know how it feels.

Mr1IvF73sl||1.situation: I slammed the kitchen cabinet shut and shouted at my wife when she tried to discuss our stepchildren’s bedtime, then I stormed out, leaving the kids unsupervised.
Mr1IvF73sl||1.thought: I realize my outburst just proved I’m incapable of holding our blended family together, and the children will grow up feeling abandoned.

persona_profile.name: Victoria
persona_profile.traits: You are an introverted and emotionally stable person. When it comes to dealing with other people, you are often antagonistic. You are always very organized when tackling problems. Further, you are very open-minded about new things.
persona_profile.persona_hub: A mother of two who is interested in learning effective communication strategies to improve harmony in her blended family.

belief.rationale: Her high self_cause (10) and self_control (7) scores show she sees herself as the source of order and believes she can prevent the house from collapsing. These appraisals refer to her normal self‑view, so the belief that she is the steady, organized parent who keeps the house on schedule existed before the clash.
belief.content: I believe that I am steady, organized parent who keeps house on schedule.

desire.rationale: Goal_incongruence (8) and unacceptable_consequences (9) indicate that any disruption to bedtime threatens her sense of safety. Therefore she already wishes that bedtime runs smoothly and the kids feel safe and orderly, a desire that predates the incident.
desire.content: I wish that bedtime runs smoothly and the kids feel safe and orderly.

intention.rationale: Coping_demand (6) together with self_control (7) shows she prepares to act to protect the schedule. Before the disagreement she intends to enforce the bedtime plan firmly and keep the schedule locked down, which later manifested as the outburst.
intention.content: I intend to enforce the bedtime plan firmly and keep the schedule locked down.

cogapp_dims.justification: Her immediate thought explicitly blames herself: she says the outburst 'proved I’m incapable' — that is clear self-attribution of the cause and failure. An average person hearing this would hear strong self-blame as the core distress.

She fears lasting harm to the children — 'the children will grow up feeling abandoned' — which signals that the consequences feel extreme and unbearable to her. This future-oriented, catastrophic worry about children's wellbeing is highly salient.

The incident directly conflicts with her prior belief and desire to be the steady, organizing parent who keeps the blended family calm. The gap between who she believes she is and what happened makes goal incongruence highly relevant.

Her statement implies a loss of control — she stormed out and now sees herself as unable to 'hold' the family together. The sense that she couldn't control her behavior and the situation is a clear part of her distress.

She likely anticipates having to repair relationships, manage guilt, and prevent future episodes — tasks that demand emotional energy and practical work. An average listener would note the burden of coping and fixing the fallout as an important secondary worry.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Good morning, Victoria. It’s nice to see you. How are you feeling today?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Hi. I’m alright, I guess. Just a bit tired.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: I hear you. Anything in particular that’s been on your mind this week?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: The house has been busy. I’ve been trying to keep everything in order, especially the kids’ bedtime.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds important to you. How have the bedtime routines been going?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I asked my wife to go over the schedule, but she kept adding her ideas. I felt the plan slipping.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: When the plan felt like it was slipping, what happened next?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I closed the kitchen cabinet hard and shouted at her. Then I left the room, and the kids were still up.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds like a strong reaction. What’s been running through your mind since then?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I keep thinking that if I can’t stay calm now, I’m not the steady parent I try to be. I worry the kids will feel like I’m abandoning them.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: You mentioned wanting to stay steady and organized. Can you tell me more about why that matters to you?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I’ve always kept the house on a schedule. When everything has a place and a time, the chaos feels less threatening.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like the schedule feels like a safety net. When that net was tugged, you felt the house might collapse.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Exactly. I thought a clear bedtime plan would let me close the cabinet without thinking about the mess outside it.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: And how did your wife’s involvement feel in that moment?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I felt like she was stepping on the plan I’d built. It made me defensive, like she didn’t trust my ability to manage things.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like there’s a fear that if you let go of a little control, the whole routine could tumble.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I know it sounds extreme, but the thought of the kids noticing me falter makes my chest feel heavy.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That heaviness you notice—does it show up only when the schedule is threatened, or also in other parts of the day?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Mostly at night. When the kids are fighting over screens and the clock is ticking, I feel the need to lock everything down.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: You’ve been very organized about bedtime. What might happen if you allowed a small part of that routine to be shared?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Part of me wonders if giving my wife one bedtime could actually give me a breather, but another part imagines the whole night falling apart.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like there are two voices: one that sees sharing as a chance for relief, and another that fears collapse. Which voice feels louder right now?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Right now the fear is louder. I can hear the kids crying upstairs and it makes the knot in my chest tighten.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Let’s try a small experiment. Imagine you let your wife handle just the first bedtime tonight. What would you notice in the kitchen while that’s happening?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I might actually have a moment to wipe the counter without hearing the shouting. It could feel like a brief pause.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That pause could be a space to notice how the house feels without you holding every lever. How does that possibility feel?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: It feels strange, like giving up a piece of control I’ve always kept. But maybe it’s not a loss, just a shift.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Shifts can be easier than losing something completely. If the shift works, what might that tell you about your role as the steady parent?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Maybe being steady isn’t about doing everything myself, but about setting the structure and letting others help keep it up.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds like a new perspective: steadiness as a framework rather than a solo performance. How could you test that idea tomorrow?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I could ask my wife to lead the 7‑year‑old’s bedtime routine and see how the night runs. I’ll keep a list of what works and what feels off.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Keeping a list fits your organized style. It also gives you concrete data instead of imagined catastrophe. Does that feel doable?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Yes. It feels less like surrender and more like adding a new piece to the plan.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Great. Let’s check in next time about how that experiment went. Thank you for sharing, Victoria.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Thank you. I’ll let you know.

XRPE6Ou7uo||1.situation: I slipped into my neighbor's empty shop using the spare key and slipped the priceless vintage cash register into my bag, then I heard frantic voices rising from the back room and felt an icy presence like a ghost watching me.
XRPE6Ou7uo||1.thought: I can feel the angry specter closing in, its fury reflecting my own betrayal, and I’m terrified that its rage will utterly consume me.

persona_profile.name: Angela
persona_profile.traits: You are an introverted and emotionally stable person. When it comes to dealing with other people, you are often agreeable. You are always very careless when tackling problems. Moreover, you are very conservative about new things.
persona_profile.persona_hub: A shop owner who firmly believes in the supernatural and claims to have encountered the resident's presence.

belief.rationale: The highest norm_violation score (9) shows Angela holds a strong conviction about not betraying others. Because this belief existed before she even thought of the spare key, the later violation feels especially shocking. It also underpins the self_cause appraisal – she knows she is the one who would break her own rule.
belief.content: I believe that I am a careful, trustworthy shopkeeper who never betrays others.

desire.rationale: Self_cause (8) and unacceptable_consequences (7) point to a pre‑existing wish to avoid the rent notice and keep the lights on. The desire for cash existed before any plan to steal, driving her to look for a practical solution.
desire.content: I wish that I could cover the rent gap and keep the lights on.

intention.rationale: Suddenness (6) and unpredictability (5) reflect that Angela formed a quick, concrete plan before stepping inside: using the spare key, taking the register, and leaving before anyone noticed. This intention was in place prior to the ghostly experience, making the situation a disruption of that plan.
intention.content: I intend to use the spare key, take the old register, and leave quietly.

cogapp_dims.justification: Her immediate thought centers on betrayal — “its fury reflecting my own betrayal.” She sees what happened as a moral violation of who she believes herself to be (a careful, trustworthy shopkeeper). An average person would hear this and say the core distress is guilt/shame from breaking her own standards.

She directly caused the situation by taking the register with intent. The thought frames the specter’s anger as a mirror of her action, so she interprets the threat as caused by her own deed. Most people would view her worry as self-blame for bringing this on herself.

Her fear that the specter’s rage will “utterly consume” her makes catastrophic consequences central. An ordinary listener would take her terror literally as dread of unbearable outcomes — punishment, being ruined, or being overwhelmed by guilt/fear.

The event was abrupt: she slipped in quietly expecting nothing, then suddenly heard frantic voices and felt an 'icy presence.' The shock and abruptness are salient — she didn’t anticipate this immediate escalation.

After the theft the situation’s outcomes are uncertain (voices, a ghostly feeling). She can’t predict what will happen next — whether she’ll be confronted, caught, or harmed — which fuels anxiety. An average person would point to the unknown consequences as worsening her fear.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Good afternoon, Angela. How are you feeling today?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Hello. I'm alright, just a little tired. The shop has been busy and the rent notice on the counter keeps catching my eye.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: I hear you. It sounds like the rent pressure is weighing on you. Anything in particular has been on your mind lately?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Well… there’s something I haven’t mentioned yet. Yesterday, I used the spare key I keep for emergencies and slipped into my neighbor’s empty shop.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds like a significant step. What were you hoping would happen when you went inside?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I thought, if I could just get the old cash register—it's a vintage piece that could be sold for a good price—I’d have enough to cover the rent gap and keep the lights on.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: So it felt like a practical solution, almost like fixing a broken shelf in the store. How did it feel when you actually opened the door?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: The lock clicked, and for a moment I imagined the register humming, the ledger balancing, the rent notice disappearing. Then, a sudden chill ran down my spine, like a draft from an empty aisle.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That cold feeling—did it feel more like an external sensation or something inside you?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: It was hard to tell. I heard faint voices from the back room, as if someone was whispering, and I got the sense that an angry presence was watching me. My hands started to shake.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like the environment amplified an inner worry. When you think about that presence now, what comes up for you?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I keep feeling a pressure on my neck, like an icy breath. It reminds me of the guilt I felt slipping the register into my bag, even though I told myself it was just a desperate move.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: You’ve described that breath as both a warning and a reflection of your own anger. How does that affect your view of yourself as a shopkeeper?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I’ve always seen myself as careful and trustworthy, keeping my inventory accurate and treating customers fairly. Now I’m questioning that image because I broke my own rule.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It’s understandable to feel unsettled when actions clash with self‑expectations. What would you like to happen next, both for the shop and for this lingering feeling?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I need cash tonight—lights are flickering, the rent notice is still on the counter, and that cold breath won’t leave me alone. I’m looking for something concrete I can do right now.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Let’s explore quick, realistic options that fit with how you usually run your store. What resources do you have at hand?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I have a small stock of best‑selling items, a loyal customer list, and a social media page that I’ve rarely used for promotions.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Great. How about announcing a 24‑hour flash sale—perhaps a buy‑one‑get‑one‑free on those top items—and sending a brief note to your regulars? You could also put simple flyers on nearby lamp posts.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I can post on the neighborhood WhatsApp group and Instagram right now, and I’ll print a few flyers. It feels urgent, but I think I can manage it.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sense of urgency is the same energy you felt when you turned the key—sharp, focused. Channeling it into a clear, organized plan might also quiet that icy breath.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Okay, I’m drafting the message: ‘24‑hour sale today—buy one, get one free on our best items. First ten customers receive a free coffee.’ I’ll post it now and start putting flyers up.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Excellent. As you take these steps, notice any changes in the pressure you feel. Sometimes, taking concrete action can transform that cold draft into a refreshing breeze.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I’ll keep an eye on it. Thank you for helping me map this out.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: You’re welcome, Angela. Let’s check in next session about how the sale went and how the feeling in your neck has shifted.

7MyCpkVx6i||1.situation: I carelessly blurted out my best friend's desperate plan to hide his crippling debt from his family to another account collector during a lunch break, treating it as idle gossip. The colleague then used that information to pressure my friend into a risky settlement that could cost him his home.
7MyCpkVx6i||1.thought: I am drowning in shame, realizing my careless slip has shattered my friend's trust and threatened his family's future. I can’t forgive myself for betraying the one person who has always counted on my discretion.

persona_profile.name: Sean
persona_profile.traits: You are an introverted and emotionally stable person. When it comes to dealing with other people, you are often agreeable. You are always very careless when tackling problems. Moreover, you are very conservative about new things.
persona_profile.persona_hub: A loyal and trustworthy best friend who offers a listening ear and valuable advice to the twin teenage daughters.

belief.rationale: The 10‑point self_cause score shows Sean saw himself as the one who must guard his friend's confidence. Because his goal was to protect the friend (high goal_incongruence when that fails) and the consequences felt unacceptable (score 8), he entered the lunch break believing he could keep the ‘inside story’ safe.
belief.content: I believe that I can keep my friend's inside story safe.

desire.rationale: Unacceptable consequences (8) and goal_incongruence (9) indicate a strong wish to avoid harming the friend’s family. Other_control (7) reminds him that others could jeopardize that safety, so before speaking he already wished the family stayed out of trouble.
desire.content: I wish that my friend's family stays out of trouble.

intention.rationale: Self_control (6) reflects Sean’s sense that he could choose whether to mention the debt, while other_control (7) acknowledges the coworker’s influence but does not override his own plan. Thus, prior to lunch he intended to keep the debt a private matter.
intention.content: I intend to keep his debt a private matter during lunch.

cogapp_dims.justification: The thought is explicitly self-blaming (“I can’t forgive myself… betrayed…”). An average person hearing this would see Sean as holding himself fully responsible for the breach of confidence — his careless slip is presented as the direct cause of the harm.

Sean’s prior belief and desire were to protect his friend’s privacy; the outcome directly contradicts that goal. His distress focuses on having failed the promise to preserve the friend’s family stability, so goal incongruence is highly salient.

The thought stresses severe fallout — “threatened his family's future,” possible loss of home — which an average person would interpret as consequences that feel unbearable or catastrophic for the friend and thus for Sean too.

Although Sean caused the leak, the colleague then used the information to pressure the friend. That other person’s actions intensified the harm and are seen as someone else exercising control over the friend’s fate, so other_control matters here.

Sean describes being careless and intended to treat it as idle chatter. He likely feels he lacked self-restraint or vigilance in that moment (low perceived self-control), which feeds his shame and sense that he could have prevented the outcome.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Hey, thanks for seeing me today. How’s your week been?

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It’s been busy, but good. I’m glad you could make it. How are you feeling as you walk in?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Honestly, I’ve been feeling kind of heavy. Something happened at lunch and I can’t stop thinking about it.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds uncomfortable. Would you like to tell me a little about what happened?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: We were on a short break, just talking about the big account we’re chasing. I mentioned my best friend’s money troubles – how he’s trying to hide a big debt – and I said it out loud, almost like I was bragging about knowing the inside story.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like that comment carried more weight than you expected. How did the coworker react?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: He started taking notes. Later he told the manager, and now my friend is being pressed into a settlement that could cost him his house. I feel like I just opened a door I never meant to.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That must feel like a big breach of trust. What’s going through your mind when you think about your friend’s situation now?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I’m drowning in shame. I always thought I could keep a friend’s secret safe. I wanted to look sharp in front of the guys, but now I’ve put his family at risk.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of self‑blame. When you think back to that moment, what were you hoping to achieve by saying those things?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I was hoping to seem knowledgeable, maybe get a quick tip about handling tough accounts. I didn’t think anyone would take it seriously – I assumed it would just be a joke.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: So the intention was to fit in and be helpful, but the outcome was far from that. How does it feel to see the gap between what you wanted and what actually happened?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: It feels like my goal and the result are on opposite sides of a line. The fact that my friend’s house could be in danger because of a careless comment makes the shame almost unbearable.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That mismatch can be really painful. What, if anything, feels within your control right now?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I can still call my friend, own up to what I said, and tell him I’m talking to the manager to try to pause the settlement. I could also ask my coworker to pull back his notes.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Those sound like concrete steps you can take. How does the idea of making that call feel for you?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Terrifying. I keep picturing him hanging up on me. But I also know staying silent will just keep the knot in my chest tighter.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It’s understandable to feel nervous. Sometimes the hardest calls are the ones that move the story forward. What might you say to keep the conversation focused on repair rather than blame?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I could start by saying I messed up, that I didn’t think about how it would affect him, and that I’m already speaking with the manager to see if we can hold off on the settlement. I’ll also mention I’m looking for a safer repayment plan for him.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds clear and responsible. How confident do you feel about setting that plan in motion tonight?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I’m still shaky, but I’ve set my phone to dial his number right after dinner. The anxiety is there, but at least I’m taking a step instead of looping in my head.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Taking that step is a sign you’re honoring the promise you made to yourself to protect your friend. After the call, we can check in on how it went and what you learned from the experience.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Thank you. I’ll make the call and then we can talk about it. I just hope he’ll hear me.

DoTKAe524E||1.situation: I stole $2,000 from the register during my shift and used it to book a weekend getaway for my wife, but the security cameras caught me and she saw the footage that night, packed her bags, and left our apartment.
DoTKAe524E||1.thought: I am a pathetic, selfish wreck who destroyed the only thing that mattered to me, and I can't see any way to ever earn back her love or my own dignity.

persona_profile.name: Diana
persona_profile.traits: You are an extroverted and emotionally unstable person. When it comes to dealing with other people, you are often agreeable. You are always very careless when tackling problems. Moreover, you are very conservative about new things.
persona_profile.persona_hub: A married individual seeking advice on whether to pursue a legal separation or try therapy first.

belief.rationale: The highest self_cause score (10) shows Diana views herself as the primary agent of protecting the marriage. Her strong self‑identity as the "steady one" who "keeps the lights on" creates a core belief that, if disrupted, yields the unacceptable consequences (9) and goal incongruence (8) observed after the theft. Because this self‑view existed prior to any action, it explains why the situation felt catastrophic and why she blamed herself entirely.
belief.content: I believe that I’m the steady one who keeps the lights on for us.

desire.rationale: The desire to have her wife feel cherished and to be seen as the "rock" aligns with the high goal_incongruence (8) and unacceptable_consequences (9): she aimed to secure the relationship through a memorable weekend. This wish existed before the act, driving her to seek a big gesture, and it explains why the failure of that wish felt so devastating.
desire.content: I wish that my wife feels cherished and sees I’m still her rock.

intention.rationale: Self_cause (10) and other_control (6) indicate Diana planned a proactive move she could control (taking cash) to influence her wife's perception (the other). The intention to "grab cash from the register and book a surprise weekend" was formed before the disruption, reflecting her pre‑situation strategy to meet her desire while protecting the relationship, which later turned into the unacceptable outcome.
intention.content: I intend to grab cash from the register and book a surprise weekend.

cogapp_dims.justification: Her central thought is self-condemnation — “I am a pathetic, selfish wreck.” That directly names herself as the cause of the disaster: she stole the money and recognizes that act produced the fallout. An average person would see her guilt and self-blame as the clearest driver of her distress.

She believes she "destroyed the only thing that mattered" — i.e., the relationship — and feels there is no way to regain love or dignity. Fear of losing everything and its perceived irreparability is the second most painful element.

Her action directly violated her prior goal/identity (being a dependable partner who secures the relationship). The outcome (wife leaving after seeing footage) conflicts sharply with her expectation that the surprise would strengthen the relationship.

While she caused the theft, her partner's reaction (seeing the footage, packing up, and leaving) is an action by someone else that determines the immediate outcome. An average listener would note she feels powerless because her wife's decision controls the relationship's fate.

The consequences unfolded in a way she likely did not expect (cameras catching her, partner seeing it that night). The unpredictability of how quickly and publicly things escalated amplifies shock and regret.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Hey, Dr. Lee. Good to see you. How's your morning going?

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Good morning, Diana. It’s a quiet start for me—just a coffee and the usual paperwork. How are you feeling today?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Honestly, kind of shaky. My shift at the store was a mess… long lines, a broken scanner, and I kept thinking about the weekend. It’s like my head just won’t stop looping.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds exhausting. When a thought keeps looping like that, it can feel like the register is stuck on the same price forever. Is there something in particular that’s looping for you right now?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Yeah… I took $2,000 from the register during my shift. I thought if I booked a surprise weekend for my wife it would show her I still have my “rock” side. The security cam caught me, she saw it that night, packed her bags and left. I keep telling myself I’m a pathetic, selfish wreck who can’t ever earn back her love or even my own dignity.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Thank you for sharing that. It sounds like you were trying to protect something you value—your marriage—by making a big gesture. Can you tell me more about what you hoped the weekend would bring for both of you?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I kept picturing us driving down the coast, staying at a cute little B&B, laughing over cheap wine. I thought if I could give her that memory, she’d see I’m still the one who can provide, even after all the extra shifts and late nights.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: So the idea of the weekend was a way to show you’re dependable, to prove you’re still keeping the roof over your heads, right?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Exactly. I always tell myself I’m the steady one at home, the guy who can keep the lights on. When the bills piled up, I felt scared that I’d look like a failure. That fear pushed me to grab the cash, even though I knew it was risky.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like the fear of not measuring up overwhelmed the practical side of you. When that fear took over, it felt safer to take a shortcut rather than face the possibility of losing that “provider” role.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Yeah, and now every time I replay that night in my head, the camera’s red light is like a spotlight on my cowardice. I see her packing, her face in the footage—she looks like a judge. I don’t even know where to start fixing it.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sentence captures the core of what you want to say without extra decoration. It acknowledges the fear, the action, and the ownership. How does it feel to have those three pieces together?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: It feels… a little less chaotic. Like instead of a tornado, it’s a single gust of wind. Still scary, but maybe I can handle one gust.

dialogue_history.content: That’s a helpful image. You’re allowing yourself to start with a small, manageable step rather than trying to rebuild the whole house at once. What might be the next small step after you send that note?

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds like a practical approach. Let’s keep exploring how you can reinforce that dependable side of yourself, not through a single grand gesture, but through steady, daily actions.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I like that. It feels more like me—a steady cashier who knows the numbers—rather than a risky gambler.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Great. Between the brief note and the repayment plan, you’re already laying the first bricks of a new foundation. We can talk more about how to stay gentle with yourself if the shame loops return.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Okay, I’ll write the note tonight and send it tomorrow. Thanks, Dr. Lee. I feel a little less stuck already.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: You’re welcome, Diana. I’m looking forward to hearing how it goes in our next session. Take care of yourself in the meantime.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That’s a heavy load to carry. It also explains why the empty chair feels louder than any clink of crystal.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I keep scrolling through photos of the glittered tables, and the one spot where his name should be is just a blank space. It’s like the whole event is a hollow echo.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: What would happen if you were to acknowledge that space openly—perhaps by reaching out to Mike and sharing what you’ve realized?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I’m terrified the note will sound like another marketing pitch. My mind is stuck on brand image, and I’m worried any genuine apology will just blur into my business voice.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It’s understandable to worry about that overlap. Maybe we can think of the note as a bridge between the two parts of you—the organized planner and the loyal friend—rather than a promotional tool.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: So, write something that’s just me, not the brand? That feels risky, but maybe it’s the only way to quiet that empty chair.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Exactly. When you write, you can keep the language simple, focus on the promise you made, and express the regret you feel for breaking it. It doesn’t have to be polished for clients; it can be raw and honest.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Alright, I’ll try that. I’ll sit down tonight and draft a note that’s just about the friendship, not the portfolio.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: We’ll check in next time on how that note goes and what it reveals for you about balancing prestige with personal integrity.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Honestly, I told myself the curtain could wait. My gut was already nagging, but I organized the edit into a checklist, ticked it off, and kept telling myself the deadline was the real spotlight. The thought that I’d be ‘the dad who stays true to his craft’ felt more respectable than a simple applause.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like you were trying to protect a belief you hold about yourself—that your cynicism exposes the nonsense around you. When the play went on without you, what went through your mind?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I kept hearing the audience’s murmurs of pity instead of the claps I imagined. It hit me that the satire I’d crafted was now a punchline aimed at my own missed bow. The irony was brutal: I mocked parental hype, yet I’d just missed the very thing I was supposed to be protecting.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds painful. You mentioned a feeling of irony—what does that feel like for you right now?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Like a spotlight turned on me, exposing a hollow shield. The column feels flat now, a cheap garnish over the real loss. I’m angry at myself for letting a deadline dictate a moment I can’t get back.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like you’re recognizing that the goal you set for the night—publishing a scathing piece—clashed with another goal, being present for your daughter. How does that clash sit with you?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: It’s a classic case of my own script beating me. I had full control over the schedule, so the mismatch feels like a personal failure. I’m also annoyed that I violated a standard I set for myself—being an organized, responsible dad.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: You’re identifying a gap between your values and your actions, which is a solid step. When you look back, do you notice any patterns in how you prioritize work over personal moments?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Mostly, I see a pattern of treating any ‘hype’—whether about parenting or news—as a battlefield. I’m quick to jump in with a satirical weapon instead of stepping off the field. It’s a habit I’ve defended with the belief that I’m providing a necessary reality check.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That habit seems tied to a deeper belief that your cynicism is a service to others. How does that belief hold up when you think about your daughter’s laughter?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: It feels shaky. I used to think the laugh would come from my audience, not my own living room. Now the thought of her giggle feels like a missing line in my column—something I can’t edit in later.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: If you could rewrite that scene, what would you want to say—or do—differently?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I’d drop the deadline at 6 p.m., walk into the auditorium, and let her have that moment. Maybe I’d even channel my sarcasm into a quick, proud comment after the show instead of a post‑deadline email.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds like a meaningful shift. What might help you make that shift the next time a deadline collides with family?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I could set a hard stop on my editing by 5 p.m., treat that as non‑negotiable, and actually schedule a ten‑minute ‘intermission’ with her. I’m not sold on a ten‑minute pause being enough, but at least it’s a concrete step.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: A concrete step is a solid start. How does setting that boundary feel in relation to your desire to maintain your voice as a columnist?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: It feels like I’m carving out a separate stage for two different audiences. My satire still gets published, but the family time gets its own headline—‘Dad Shows Up.’ It’s a different kind of impact, but maybe it’s one that actually matters.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like you’re creating a new script where both parts of you can be heard. How confident do you feel about trying that out this week?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I’m nervous, because the inbox will still ping, but I’m also oddly excited. If I can sit with the irritation and still choose the backstage laugh, maybe the ‘punchline’ won’t feel like a verdict on my dad‑hood after all.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That willingness to sit with the discomfort while choosing presence is a powerful move. Let’s keep checking in on how that feels for you next time we talk.

dialogue_history.content: Hey Jonathan, good to see you. How's everything going today?

dialogue_history.content: Got it. A long stretch away can feel heavy. Anything on your mind as you get ready?

dialogue_history.content: And after you posted, what was the response?

dialogue_history.content: That quiet must have been hard. What does it bring up for you right now?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I’m overwhelmed by shame. I keep thinking I broke the only real bond I had with them. I feel lonely, like I’m carrying the weight of that mistake while I’m already swamped with packing boxes.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: You mentioned feeling responsible. How does that sit with your idea of yourself as a loyal friend?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: It clashes. I always thought I’d never betray a friend’s trust. Posting that private video feels like I stepped over a line I never meant to cross.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: So the action didn’t line up with your goal of staying close to them, and it also broke a personal rule you hold.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Exactly. I wanted their approval, a little buzz, but I ignored the fact that it was private. Now the silence feels like a mirror, showing how low I’ve sunk.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like you’re weighing two options: send a quick note to explain, or wait until you’re back and hope things smooth over on their own. What’s pulling you toward each choice?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: If I apologize now, I’m scared it’ll sound fake and make the silence louder. Waiting feels like I’m waiting for the night shift to end, but I also worry I’ll walk back in and everyone will see me as the guy who messed up.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Imagine you write a short, honest line—just a heads‑up that you didn’t mean to overstep. It could be a bridge rather than a plea. How does that idea sit with you?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I guess it could be less dramatic. Maybe saying, “Hey, I posted that video without thinking. Sorry if it crossed a line,” would show I care without over‑apologizing.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds like a balanced approach. It acknowledges your role, respects their feelings, and keeps the door open for connection when you return.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Alright. I’ll try that. Thanks.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Hey, Dr. Miller. How’s your day going?

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Hi Andrew, thanks for asking. It’s been good, and I’m glad you’re here. How are you feeling as we start today?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Honestly, pretty wound up. I’ve been up all night feeding the baby, the house is quiet only when she’s asleep, and I’ve been feeling like I’m running on empty.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds exhausting. It makes sense you’d be looking for a little breather. What have you been hoping a short break would give you?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Just a few minutes to step outside, clear my head – maybe chat with other parents at that late‑night parents’ club we heard about. I thought I could keep the baby close, keep the sleeper lid shut, and still get a bit of air.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: So you imagined a quick escape that wouldn’t disturb her sleep. When you got there, what was it really like?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: The place was packed, lights flickering, bass thumping like a truck. I was cracking jokes, trying to be the life of the room, and the whole floor shook. The sleeper lid slammed shut on her head and she let out this terrified scream that ripped through the hallway.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like the sound hit you hard, both literally and emotionally. What’s been running through your mind since that moment?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I keep hearing that little scream echo in my head. It feels like bile bubbling up—‘I ruined another night of her sleep, I’m a selfish, careless idiot.’ I can’t shake the thought that I’ve let her down, and that my wife will think I’m the cause of her exhaustion too.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: I hear a lot of pain and self‑criticism there. When you think back to before you left the house, what belief were you relying on to make that decision?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I kept telling myself I was a careful dad, that a short break wouldn’t hurt her. I wanted to prove to myself I could still be a good parent while getting a breath.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like the outcome clashed sharply with that belief, which is why the guilt feels so intense. Let’s explore how that clash is affecting you right now.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I feel jittery, like I’m walking on a tightrope. Every time I think about taking a minute for myself, I picture the bass, the lid snapping, her scream—again. I’m scared to try anything new, even simple things like a fan or a neighbor watching.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That fear of trying something new makes sense, especially when you’ve just had a painful experience. What might a small, familiar step look like for you, something that feels safe but still gives you a brief pause?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Maybe just putting a soft blanket over the crib and leaving the door half‑closed while I sit on the couch for five minutes, with my wife nearby. No music, no club vibe—just the TV at low volume.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds like a concrete, low‑risk plan that stays within what feels familiar. How would you check in with yourself during those five minutes to make sure you’re staying calm?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I could focus on my breathing, count each inhale, maybe hum a quiet tune I used to sing to her. If I start to hear the club in my head, I’d bring my attention back to the hum.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Great. Keeping the focus on a gentle, repeatable sound can act like a lighthouse when intrusive thoughts swirl. How does that plan feel compared to the idea of stepping out to the club?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: It feels safer, like I’m not throwing a wild card into the mix. I’m still giving myself a minute, but I’m not risking a loud bass or a snapping lid.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Excellent. Let’s try this for the next few evenings and see how it goes. We’ll revisit how you feel after each try, and we can adjust if needed. How does that sound?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Sounds good. I’ll give it a shot and let you know what happens. Thanks for hearing me out.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: You’re welcome, Andrew. I’m proud of you for taking this step. I’ll see you next week to talk about how the five‑minute pause went.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Good morning, Cameron. How are you feeling today?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Morning. Honestly, a bit bruised. Sales have been flat for weeks and the back‑room feels like a maze of unsold stock.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That sounds stressful. When the numbers don’t move, it can feel like the whole operation is stuck.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Exactly. I keep replaying the same question: how do I get one quick infusion of cash without adding another line to the ledger?

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: You’ve mentioned looking for a fast boost. What did you decide to try?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I ran into the clerk at the corner store who seemed nervous, and I kind of coaxed him into slipping me a small package that wasn’t theirs. I told my junior associate to tuck it under the new dresses in the boutique, thinking it would disappear into the existing inventory.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That’s a bold move. Can you tell me what was going through your mind as you arranged that?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I told myself it was just one discreet item—nothing that would change the way I run the shop. It felt like a temporary lever to keep the cash flow from stalling.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: So the idea was that a single, hidden addition would shore up the numbers without upsetting the overall balance?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Right. I’ve always prided myself on keeping the team honest, and I thought I could control this little slip, keep it invisible, and move on.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Now that it’s in place, what’s come up for you?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: It sounds like the image of the hidden box is acting like a reminder of something that conflicts with your core standards.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Exactly. I keep asking myself why I believed a stolen package could solve months of low sales. It feels like I’ve stepped off the path I set for the business.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: You mentioned earlier that you value organization. How does that value play into what’s happening right now?

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: I’m usually meticulous—labels, inventory sheets, everything in its right place. Yet here I am, hiding something that throws a wrench into that order. It feels like I’ve introduced chaos into a system I built to avoid it.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: That tension between your organized side and this hidden element could be amplifying the anxiety.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: And the worst part is I don’t know who else is pulling strings now. The clerk was nervous, my junior is curious, and I can’t predict how this will ripple.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: So there’s a sense that the outcome feels out of your control, even though you initiated it.

dialogue_history.speaker: Patient
dialogue_history.content: Yes. It’s like I opened a door I can’t shut, and every time I hear the fridge hum or the lights flicker, I imagine that door widening.

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: If we treated that hidden box as a signal rather than a secret, what practical step could you take that aligns with your need for order?

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Turning the unknown into a known quantity could reduce the anxiety loop. How might you approach that conversation with your junior?

dialogue_history.speaker: Therapist
dialogue_history.content: Your willingness to be transparent could also reinforce the integrity you value, showing that even when you stumble, you can steer the ship back on course.

dialogue_history.content: Taking that step could transform the humming fridge into the background noise of a well‑run boutique rather than a warning alarm.
